questions.stem: The contrapositive of “If P, then Q” is:
options: If Q, then P
If not P, then not Q
If P, then not Q
If not Q, then not P
questions.explanation: The contrapositive swaps the two parts and negates both, and it is logically equivalent to the original. “If Q, then P” is the converse and “If not P, then not Q” is the inverse; neither is equivalent to the original.

questions.stem: The converse of “If n is divisible by 6, then n is divisible by 3” is:
options: If n is divisible by 3, then n is divisible by 6
If n is not divisible by 3, then n is not divisible by 6
If n is not divisible by 6, then n is not divisible by 3
n is divisible by 6 if and only if n is divisible by 3
questions.explanation: The converse of “If P, then Q” is “If Q, then P”. Here the converse is false (n = 3 is a counter-example) while the original is true. The statement with both parts negated and swapped is the contrapositive, not the converse.

questions.stem: The negation of “For all real numbers x, x² ≥ x” is:
options: For all real numbers x, x² ≤ x
There exists a real number x such that x² < x
For all real numbers x, x² < x
There exists a real number x such that x² ≥ x
questions.explanation: Negating “for all” gives “there exists”, and the inequality is negated: not (x² ≥ x) is x² < x. Keeping “for all” and reversing the inequality makes a much stronger claim than the negation; x = 1/2 shows the negation is true.

questions.stem: The statement “P is a sufficient condition for Q” means that:
options: P and Q are equivalent
P implies Q
Q implies P
not P implies not Q
questions.explanation: A sufficient condition is enough on its own: whenever P holds, Q holds, so P implies Q. “Q implies P” would make P a necessary condition for Q, and equivalence would need both directions.

questions.stem: A proof by contradiction that √2 is irrational begins by assuming that:
options: 2 is the square of an even integer
√2 = a/b, where a and b are both even integers
√2 = a/b, where a and b are integers with no common factor
√2 cannot be written as a fraction of two integers
questions.explanation: A proof by contradiction assumes the negation of what is to be proved, so it assumes √2 is rational, written in lowest terms. The proof then shows a and b are both even, which contradicts their having no common factor.

questions.stem: In a proof by mathematical induction that P(n) is true for all n ∈ N, the inductive step shows that:
options: if P(k) is true, then P(k + 1) is true
P(k + 1) is true for every k ∈ N
P(1) is true
if P(k + 1) is true, then P(k) is true
questions.explanation: The inductive step proves the implication P(k) → P(k + 1) for an arbitrary k. Checking P(1) is the base case, a separate step. Proving P(k + 1) outright for every k would be proving the whole result without induction.

questions.stem: The statement “P if and only if Q” means:
options: Q implies P, but P need not imply Q
P implies Q, and Q implies P
P implies Q, but Q need not imply P
P and Q are both true
questions.explanation: “If and only if” joins an implication and its converse: P is both necessary and sufficient for Q. It says P and Q have the same truth value, which can mean both are false.

questions.stem: Which value of n proves the statement “There exists an integer n such that n² = 2n”?
questions.explanation: An existence statement is proved by one example: 2² = 4 = 2 × 2. For n = 1, n² = 1 but 2n = 2; for n = −2, n² = 4 but 2n = −4; and for n = 4, 16 ≠ 8.

questions.stem: In mathematics, a conjecture is:
options: a statement that has been proved from axioms
a statement accepted without proof as a starting point
an example that shows a general statement is false
a statement put forward to be proved or disproved
questions.explanation: A conjecture is a claim that has not yet been settled. A proved statement is a theorem, a statement accepted without proof is an axiom, and a single example showing a statement fails is a counter-example.

questions.stem: To prove that n(n + 1) is even for every integer n, a student treats n even and n odd separately. This method is:
options: proof by cases
proof by contrapositive
proof by contradiction
proof by mathematical induction
questions.explanation: Splitting into cases that together cover every integer is proof by cases. If n = 2m, then n(n + 1) = 2m(2m + 1); if n = 2m + 1, then n(n + 1) = (2m + 1)(2m + 2) = 2(2m + 1)(m + 1). Both are even.

questions.stem: In a proof by contradiction of a statement P, the student:
options: finds one example for which P fails
assumes not P and deduces something known to be false
assumes P and deduces something known to be true
assumes the conclusion is false and deduces the hypothesis is false
questions.explanation: Proof by contradiction assumes the statement is false and reasons to an impossibility, so the assumption must be wrong. Assuming the conclusion false and deducing the hypothesis false is proof by contrapositive, and a single failing example disproves a statement rather than proving it.

questions.stem: Which formula for 1² + 2² + 3² + … + n² can be proved by mathematical induction?
options: n²(n + 1)²/4
questions.explanation: Only a true formula can be proved. Checking n = 2: 1 + 4 = 5, and 2 × 3 × 5/6 = 5. The formula n(n + 1)/2 sums 1 + 2 + … + n, n²(n + 1)²/4 sums the cubes, and n(n + 1)(n + 2)/6 gives 4 at n = 2.

questions.stem: If m = 2a + 1 and n = 2b + 1 for integers a and b, a direct proof that mn is odd writes mn as:
options: 4ab + 1
2(2ab + a + b)
questions.explanation: Expanding gives mn = 4ab + 2a + 2b + 1 = 2(2ab + a + b) + 1, which is one more than an even number. Writing 4ab + 1 drops the cross terms 2a and 2b.

questions.stem: The sum ∑(2k − 1), from k = 1 to k = 5, equals:
questions.explanation: The terms are 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 25, which is 5². Subtracting 1 only once from 2(1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5) = 30 gives 29, and 36 and 16 come from stopping at the wrong term.

questions.stem: To prove “If 3n + 2 is odd, then n is odd” by contrapositive, a student proves:
options: If n is even, then 3n + 2 is odd
If n is even, then 3n + 2 is even
If n is odd, then 3n + 2 is odd
If 3n + 2 is even, then n is even
questions.explanation: The contrapositive of “if P then Q” is “if not Q then not P”: if n is not odd, then 3n + 2 is not odd. With n = 2m, 3n + 2 = 2(3m + 1), which is even. “If n is odd, then 3n + 2 is odd” is the converse.

questions.stem: The statement “If x > 2, then x² > 4” is true for real x. Which value of x is a counter-example to its converse?
questions.explanation: The converse is “If x² > 4, then x > 2”. For x = −3, x² = 9 > 4 but x is not greater than 2. For x = 2 and x = −1 the hypothesis x² > 4 is false, so they cannot be counter-examples.

questions.stem: Which statement is logically equivalent to “If a quadrilateral is a square, then its diagonals are equal in length”?
options: If a quadrilateral is not a square, its diagonals are not equal
A quadrilateral is a square exactly when its diagonals are equal
If its diagonals are not equal, a quadrilateral is not a square
If its diagonals are equal, a quadrilateral is a square
questions.explanation: Only the contrapositive is equivalent to an implication. The converse and the inverse are both false here, since a rectangle that is not a square has equal diagonals.

questions.stem: Which statement about real numbers x is true?
options: x = 3 is a necessary and sufficient condition for x² = 9
x = 3 is neither necessary nor sufficient for x² = 9
x = 3 is a sufficient but not necessary condition for x² = 9
x = 3 is a necessary but not sufficient condition for x² = 9
questions.explanation: If x = 3 then x² = 9, so the condition is sufficient. It is not necessary, because x = −3 also gives x² = 9. Necessary and sufficient would need x² = 9 to force x = 3.

questions.stem: The negation of “For all integers n, if n is prime, then n is odd” is:
options: For all integers n, if n is prime, then n is even
There exists an integer n that is not prime and is odd
For all integers n, if n is not prime, then n is even
There exists a prime integer n that is even
questions.explanation: The negation of “for all n, P implies Q” is “there exists n with P and not Q”: a prime that is not odd. This negation is true (n = 2), so the original statement is false. Swapping “odd” for “even” inside the “for all” is not a negation.

questions.stem: The negation of “There exists x ∈ R such that x² + 1 = 0” is:
options: There exists x ∈ R such that x² + 1 ≠ 0
For all x ∈ R, x² + 1 = 0
There exists no x ∈ C such that x² + 1 = 0
For all x ∈ R, x² + 1 ≠ 0
questions.explanation: Negating “there exists” gives “for all”, and the equation becomes ≠. The negation is true, since x² + 1 ≥ 1 for real x. The last statement changes the set to C, where x = i is a solution.

questions.stem: A student will prove that 2^n > n² for all integers n ≥ 5 by mathematical induction. The base case checks:
questions.explanation: The base case is the first value in the claimed range, n = 5, where 2⁵ = 32 > 25. The inequality is false at n = 2, 3 and 4 (for example 16 > 16 fails), so starting from n = 1 would not lead to a valid proof.

questions.stem: In proving 1 + 3 + 5 + … + (2n − 1) = n² by induction, a student assumes the result for n = k. The inductive step must show that k² + (2k + 1) equals:
options: k² + 1
questions.explanation: The next odd number after 2k − 1 is 2(k + 1) − 1 = 2k + 1, and the target is the formula with n = k + 1, which is (k + 1)². Indeed k² + 2k + 1 = (k + 1)².

questions.stem: To prove 5^n − 1 is divisible by 4 for all n ∈ N, a student assumes 5^k − 1 = 4m for an integer m. Then 5^(k + 1) − 1 equals:
questions.explanation: 5^(k + 1) − 1 = 5 × 5^k − 1 = 5(4m + 1) − 1 = 20m + 4 = 4(5m + 1), a multiple of 4. Writing 5(4m) − 1 replaces 5^k with 4m and loses the +1 from 5^k = 4m + 1.

questions.stem: A student proves “If mn is even, then m is even or n is even” by assuming m and n are both odd and showing mn is odd. This is a proof by:
options: contradiction
cases
counter-example
contrapositive
questions.explanation: The negation of “m is even or n is even” is “m and n are both odd”, and the negation of “mn is even” is “mn is odd”. Proving not Q implies not P is proof by contrapositive. A contradiction proof would also assume mn is even.

questions.stem: A direct proof that a² + b² ≥ 2ab for all real numbers a and b starts from which true statement?
options: a² ≥ 0 and b² ≥ 0
a + b ≥ 2√(ab)
questions.explanation: Expanding (a − b)² ≥ 0 gives a² − 2ab + b² ≥ 0, which rearranges to the result. (a + b)² ≥ 0 only gives a² + b² ≥ −2ab, and a + b ≥ 2√(ab) is not even defined when ab < 0.

questions.stem: Let S(n) = 1/(1 × 2) + 1/(2 × 3) + … + 1/(n(n + 1)). From S(1), S(2) and S(3), the formula for S(n) to prove by induction is:
questions.explanation: S(1) = 1/2, S(2) = 1/2 + 1/6 = 2/3 and S(3) = 2/3 + 1/12 = 3/4, matching n/(n + 1). The formula 1/(n + 1) fits n = 1 but gives 1/3 at n = 2, which shows why one case is not enough.

questions.stem: A student conjectures that |z + w| = |z| + |w| for all complex numbers z and w. Which pair is a counter-example?
options: z = i, w = 2i
questions.explanation: For z = 1 and w = −1, |z + w| = 0 but |z| + |w| = 2. In the other pairs one number is a positive real multiple of the other (or zero), so the moduli add exactly and the equation holds.

questions.stem: Conjecture: if f′(a) = 0, then f has a local maximum or a local minimum at x = a. Which function is a counter-example at a = 0?
options: f(x) = x³ + x
f(x) = x³
f(x) = x²
f(x) = −x²
questions.explanation: f(x) = x³ has f′(0) = 0 but a stationary point of inflection at the origin, so the conjecture fails. For x³ + x, f′(0) = 1, so the hypothesis is false and it cannot be a counter-example.

questions.stem: A student checks that n² − n + 11 is prime for n = 1, 2, …, 10 and concludes that it is prime for all n ∈ N. Which comment is correct?
options: It is false, since n = 5 gives 31, which is composite
It is true for odd n only, since even n give even values
It is false, since n = 11 gives 121 = 11²
It is true, since ten checked cases establish it
questions.explanation: At n = 11 the value is 121 − 11 + 11 = 121 = 11², so one counter-example disproves the claim. Checking cases never proves a “for all” statement, however many are checked; 31 is prime and every value of n² − n + 11 is odd.

questions.stem: For a function f and a real number a, how are “f is differentiable at x = a” and “f is continuous at x = a” related?
options: Each implies the other
Neither implies the other
Differentiable implies continuous, but not conversely
Continuous implies differentiable, but not conversely
questions.explanation: Every function differentiable at a point is continuous there. The converse fails: f(x) = |x| is continuous at x = 0 but has no derivative there, so the two conditions are not equivalent.

questions.stem: To prove that n² leaves remainder 0 or 1 when divided by 4, the most natural cases to consider are:
options: n even and n odd
n prime and n composite
n positive and n negative
n < 4 and n ≥ 4
questions.explanation: If n = 2m then n² = 4m², remainder 0; if n = 2m + 1 then n² = 4(m² + m) + 1, remainder 1. Splitting by sign or size does not give a form that can be squared and divided by 4.

questions.stem: A student argues: “If n is divisible by 4, then n is even. The number 6 is even, so 6 is divisible by 4.” The error is:
options: using a single example in place of a proof
assuming the converse of a true implication
assuming the contrapositive of a true implication
assuming the negation of a true implication
questions.explanation: The argument uses “if n is even, then n is divisible by 4”, the converse, which is false. The contrapositive (if n is odd, it is not divisible by 4) is a valid deduction, so using it would not be an error.

questions.stem: In the proof that √3 is irrational, assume √3 = a/b in lowest terms, so a² = 3b². Which contradiction does the proof reach?
options: a and b are both multiples of 3
a and b are both even
b² = 3a²
a = 3 and b = 1
questions.explanation: From a² = 3b², 3 divides a², so 3 divides a. Writing a = 3c gives 9c² = 3b², so b² = 3c² and 3 divides b. Then a and b share the factor 3, contradicting lowest terms. Evenness is the argument for √2, not √3.

questions.stem: For an integer n, the condition “n is divisible by 2” is ___ for “n is divisible by 4”.
options: sufficient but not necessary
both necessary and sufficient
neither necessary nor sufficient
necessary but not sufficient
questions.explanation: Every multiple of 4 is even, so being even is necessary for divisibility by 4. It is not sufficient, because 6 is even but not divisible by 4. Students often swap the words: the sufficient condition is the one that implies the other.

questions.stem: Euclid’s proof assumes there are finitely many primes, multiplies them all together and adds 1 to get N. Why is this a contradiction?
options: N leaves remainder 1 on division by each listed prime, yet N has a prime factor
N is always itself a prime, and it is not on the list
N is even, so it is divisible by 2 and by no other prime
N is larger than every listed prime, so N must be prime
questions.explanation: Every integer greater than 1 has a prime factor, but none of the listed primes divides N, so the list was incomplete. N need not be prime itself: 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 11 × 13 + 1 = 30 031 = 59 × 509.

questions.stem: Which statement is true?
options: For every real x, x² > 0
There exists a real x such that x² < 0
For every real x, there exists a real y such that y > x²
There exists a real y such that, for every real x, y > x²
questions.explanation: Given any x, take y = x² + 1. Swapping the quantifiers asks for one y that beats every x², which fails because x² is unbounded. The statement x² > 0 fails at x = 0, and no real square is negative.

questions.stem: For n ≥ 2, the partial product (1 − 1/2²)(1 − 1/3²)(1 − 1/4²) … (1 − 1/n²) equals:
questions.explanation: Each factor is (k − 1)(k + 1)/k², and the product telescopes to (1/n) × ((n + 1)/2) = (n + 1)/(2n). Check n = 2: 3/4; n = 3: 3/4 × 8/9 = 2/3 = 4/6. The formula (n − 1)/n gives 1/2 at n = 2.

questions.stem: The largest integer that divides n³ − n for every integer n is:
questions.explanation: n³ − n = (n − 1)n(n + 1) is a product of three consecutive integers, so it contains a multiple of 2 and a multiple of 3, and 6 divides it. At n = 2 the value is 6, so no larger integer always divides it; 2 and 3 divide it but are not the largest.

questions.stem: A student “proves” by induction that n² + n + 1 is even for all n ∈ N. The inductive step, from k to k + 1, is correct. What is wrong?
options: The inductive step should show that P(k − 1) implies P(k)
The base case fails, since 1² + 1 + 1 = 3 is odd
The inductive step must assume the result for all n ≤ k
Induction cannot be used for statements about parity
questions.explanation: Adding 2k + 2 to an even number gives an even number, so the step is valid, but the statement never starts: n² + n + 1 = n(n + 1) + 1 is always odd. Both the base case and the inductive step are needed.

questions.stem: To prove that log₂(3) is irrational, a student assumes log₂(3) = p/q for positive integers p and q. This leads to:
options: p = 3q/2, so p cannot be an integer
2^q = 3^p, but one side is even and the other is odd
2^p = 3^q, but one side is even and the other is odd
3^p = 2^q, but one side is odd and the other is even
questions.explanation: From 2^(p/q) = 3, raise both sides to the power q to get 2^p = 3^q. With p ≥ 1 the left side is even, while every power of 3 is odd. Writing 3^p = 2^q or 2^q = 3^p puts the indices on the wrong bases.

questions.stem: Which “if and only if” statement about integers n is true?
options: n is divisible by 4 if and only if n² is divisible by 4
n > 1 if and only if n² > 1
n is divisible by 6 if and only if n is divisible by 3
n is odd if and only if n² is odd
questions.explanation: Odd times odd is odd, and if n is even then n² is even, so both directions hold. Each of the others fails in one direction: n = 2 gives n² = 4, n = −2 gives n² > 1, and n = 3 is divisible by 3 but not 6.

questions.stem: The negation of “For every ε > 0, there exists n ∈ N such that 1/n < ε” is:
options: There exists ε > 0 such that, for all n ∈ N, 1/n ≥ ε
For every ε > 0 and every n ∈ N, 1/n ≥ ε
There exist ε > 0 and n ∈ N such that 1/n ≥ ε
For every ε ≤ 0, there exists n ∈ N such that 1/n ≥ ε
questions.explanation: Each quantifier flips, “for every” to “there exists” and back, and the final inequality is negated. The condition ε > 0 restricts the variable and stays as it is; changing it to ε ≤ 0 is a common slip.

questions.stem: A student proves that P(1) is true and that P(k) implies P(k + 2) for every k ∈ N. Which conclusion follows?
options: P(n) is true for every natural number n
P(n) is true for every even natural number n
P(n) is true for n = 1 and n = 3 only
P(n) is true for every odd natural number n
questions.explanation: From P(1) the step gives P(3), then P(5), and so on through every odd number. Nothing reaches P(2), so the even cases need a second base case. The chain does not stop at 3, because the step applies for every k.
